replace_subtopics.title: Restate and clarify the goal
replace_subtopics.body:
Start by saying the problem back in your own words and asking what "better" means. This shows you listen, and it often reveals that the stated ask is a guess at a solution.

Ask a few clarifying questions: Why now? What happens if nothing changes? How do they measure the problem today? Which part of the organisation is involved?

Do not propose any technology yet. Interviewers watch for candidates who design too early. Customers do too.

Signpost your structure before you dive in. Say it out loud: "First I will ask a few questions, then map how discharge works today, then check the data, then pick a metric, then propose a first step and the risks." This tells the interviewer where you are going and makes it easy for them to redirect you.

Time-box the round the same way. A 30 to 45 minute case can be split as: about 5 minutes of questions, 10 minutes on the current state, 10 minutes on the design, 5 minutes on metrics and risks, and a few minutes to sum up. Glance at the clock at each switch. Running out of time before you reach a metric or a first step is one of the most common ways to fail a case round.
replace_subtopics.example: Prompt: "A regional hospital wants AI to reduce discharge delays." You restate: "So the goal is to shorten the time between a patient being medically ready to leave and actually leaving, which frees beds. Is that right, and is this across all wards or specific ones?" The interviewer says the COO is worried because the emergency department is boarding patients who wait for beds. Now you know the real driver is bed capacity. Before asking anything else you say: "I will spend about five minutes on questions, ten on how discharge works today, ten on a first solution and five on risks and metrics. Stop me if you want me to go deeper anywhere."
replace_subtopics.code:
Clarifying questions template

Goal        : What outcome would make this a success in 6 months?
Why now     : What changed? What does the problem cost today?
Scope       : Which sites, teams, products or wards?
Measure     : How is the problem measured now, if at all?
Sponsor     : Who asked for this, and who approves the budget?
Tried before: What has been tried, and why did it not work?

Signposting and time box (40-minute round)

00-05  Clarify goal, scope, sponsor        "First, a few questions..."
05-15  Users and current workflow          "Now let me map how it works today..."
15-25  Data, constraints, first design     "Given that data, here is a first slice..."
25-32  Metric, baseline, guardrail, cost   "We would know it worked if..."
32-37  Risks and next steps                "The biggest risks are..."
37-40  Summary in three sentences

replace_subtopics.title: Data reality and constraints
replace_subtopics.body:
Ask what data exists, where it lives, how fresh it is, and who can grant access. Much important information sits in free-text notes, spreadsheets or whiteboards, and some is not recorded at all.

Data access is often the slowest part of a real project. Start the access request on day one.

Then list constraints before you design: privacy law (HIPAA for US health data), where the system must run (on-premises, the customer's cloud account, or a vendor cloud), required humans in the loop, integration limits, budget and timeline. Constraints narrow the design space and show the interviewer you have done this before.

Interviewers often ask "what would this cost to run?" or "how fast must it be?". Answer with a back-of-envelope sizing line: volume times tokens times price, plus a latency budget. You do not need exact prices. Say which numbers are assumptions and round them. Tokens are the small text pieces a language model reads and writes, and providers charge per million tokens (see the llmcost concept for the full method).

The latency budget is how long the result may take. A nightly batch list can take minutes. A suggestion shown while a nurse types must come back in a second or two. The budget changes the design: a slow, cheap batch job and a fast, interactive call are different systems.
replace_subtopics.example: Discharge orders and medication lists are in the EHR and available through a read-only reporting database refreshed every 15 minutes. "Likely discharge tomorrow" exists only in physicians' progress notes as free text. Transport bookings are in a separate scheduling tool. Constraints: patient data must stay inside the hospital's cloud account, every AI suggestion must be confirmed by a nurse, and the EHR team will not allow writes into the EHR in the first phase. Quick sizing out loud: "The ward has about 32 patients. If we read about 10 notes each at roughly 2,000 tokens a note, that is 640,000 input tokens a night. At an assumed 3 dollars per million input tokens that is about 2 dollars a night, roughly 60 dollars a month for one ward. The list only has to be ready by 8 pm, so latency is not a constraint; we can run it as a batch job."

replace_subtopics.title: Success metric, baseline and guardrail
replace_subtopics.body:
Pick one primary metric that the sponsor cares about and that your work can move. Measure its baseline, the value before you change anything. Without a baseline you cannot prove impact.

Add a guardrail metric, which must not get worse. It stops you from "winning" in a harmful way, such as rushing patients out.

If possible, compare the pilot group with a similar control group over the same period. This separates your effect from seasonal changes or other projects.

The hours metric is a lagging metric: it moves only after weeks of use. Add a leading metric that shows early whether people use the tool at all. Here that is adoption: the share of nightly lists that the charge nurse opens and confirms. If adoption is low in week 2, the hours metric will not move in week 8, so you fix adoption first.
replace_subtopics.example: Primary metric: median hours from medically ready to discharge on ward 4 West. Baseline over the last 90 days: 6.5 hours. Guardrail: 30-day readmission rate, baseline 11.2%. Control: ward 5 West, similar patient mix. Target agreed with the COO: 1.5 hours saved on the pilot ward within 8 weeks with no rise in readmissions. The small calculation below turns the target into beds, which is the language the sponsor uses. Leading metric: the charge nurse opened and confirmed 17 of the 20 nightly lists in the first four weeks, 85% adoption, so it is fair to judge the hours metric at week 8.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Translate hours saved into bed capacity for the sponsor
discharges_per_day = 14          # ward 4 West average
hours_saved_each   = 1.5         # target reduction in median delay
bed_hours_per_day  = 24

bed_hours_freed = discharges_per_day * hours_saved_each
beds_equivalent = bed_hours_freed / bed_hours_per_day
print(f"{bed_hours_freed:.0f} bed-hours/day = {beds_equivalent:.2f} beds on one ward")

# Across 10 similar wards if the pilot scales
print(f"Hospital-wide: {beds_equivalent * 10:.1f} beds")

# Leading metric: adoption of the nightly list
lists_published = 20             # nights in the first 4 weeks
lists_confirmed = 17             # opened and confirmed by the charge nurse
print(f"Adoption: {lists_confirmed / lists_published:.0%}")
# Output:
# 21 bed-hours/day = 0.88 beds on one ward
# Hospital-wide: 8.8 beds
# Adoption: 85%

replace_subtopics.title: Thin slice, plan and risks
replace_subtopics.body:
A thin slice is the smallest version that solves one real problem for real users end to end. It is narrow in scope, but it works in production conditions with real data.

Pick the slice at the bottleneck. Describe what users see, what data it uses, and how a human stays in control. Give a short week-by-week plan with a demo point.

Close with the top risks and one mitigation each. Common risks are data access delays, users not trusting the tool, model errors, and scope creep. Then explain how the slice would expand if it works.

Before you propose AI, ask: do we even need AI? Name the simplest non-AI fix first. Here, the EHR could notify pharmacy automatically the moment a discharge order is drafted, not only when it is signed. That costs little and may win back part of the delay. Treat it as the baseline the AI slice must beat. If the AI list cannot beat the simple fix by a clear margin, recommend the simple fix. Interviewers reward this honesty.

A backtest target such as "80% of next-day discharges appear on the list" measures recall only: how many real discharges you caught. Also set a precision target: of the patients on the list, how many really leave the next day. Each error type has a cost. A missed discharge (false negative) means pharmacy starts late, which is today's problem. A listed patient who stays (false positive) means pharmacy reconciles medicines for nothing, which wastes their time and erodes trust. Size both in pharmacist hours.
replace_subtopics.example: Slice: each evening, a model reads progress notes and orders on 4 West and produces a list of patients likely to be discharged tomorrow. Pharmacy gets the list and starts medication reconciliation early. A charge nurse confirms or removes each name. Weeks 1 to 2: access and baseline. Weeks 3 to 4: build the list and test on past data. Week 5: demo to COO and pharmacy lead. Weeks 6 to 8: live pilot. Risks: data access (mitigation: start the request on day one), nurse trust (show reasons for each prediction), wrong predictions (nurse confirms, and overrides become eval data). Non-AI baseline: auto-notify pharmacy when the order is drafted, piloted on 5 West. AI slice target: recall of at least 80% and precision of at least 70%. With 14 discharges a day, 70% precision means about 16 names on the list and about 5 wasted reconciliations, roughly 5 x 20 minutes = 100 minutes of pharmacist time a day. Pharmacy agrees that is acceptable only if the early start saves more than that.

Wk 3-4  Build nightly list from notes + orders; backtest on 60 days
        Target: 80% of next-day discharges appear on the list
Wk 5    Demo to COO, pharmacy lead, charge nurses; adjust
Wk 6-8  Live pilot; nurse confirms each name; weekly metric review

Baseline to beat  non-AI rule: notify pharmacy when order is drafted

add_glossary: Signposting
Telling the listener the structure of your answer before you give it, so they can follow and redirect you.
Leading metric
An early signal, such as adoption, that predicts whether the main (lagging) result will move later.
Precision and recall
Recall is the share of real cases you caught; precision is the share of your flagged cases that were real.
Back-of-envelope sizing
A rough estimate from a few rounded numbers, such as volume x tokens x price, said out loud to check feasibility.
add_practice: For your practice case, write one back-of-envelope cost line (volume x tokens x price) and one non-AI fix that the AI solution must beat, then state a recall and a precision target and the cost of each error type.

add_subtopics.title: Quantitative discovery: sizing the pain with data
add_subtopics.body:
Interviews tell you what people feel. System data tells you how often it really happens. Good discovery uses both and compares them. This is called triangulation: checking one source against another. People remember the most painful or most recent case, not the most common one, so a loud complaint can be rare and a quiet one can eat most of the time.

Ask for exports that already exist: helpdesk tickets, exception queues, audit logs, email volumes by folder, the ERP's list of rejected documents. Then run simple counts: how many per week, which reason is most common, how long each type takes. Totals and percentages are enough at this stage. You are sizing the problem, not building a model.

Request data safely. Ask for the smallest sample that answers your question, for example 90 days and only the columns you need. Ask the data owner to mask names, emails and account numbers before sending, or to let you query inside their environment. Confirm that an NDA (non-disclosure agreement) and, where personal data is involved, a data processing agreement are in place. Write down where the file is stored and when you will delete it.

When the numbers and the interviews disagree, go back to the users with the numbers. The conversation that follows is often the most useful of the whole discovery.
add_subtopics.example: At the logistics company the clerks said handwritten PO numbers were the worst part of invoice entry. You ask the AP lead for a masked 90-day export of exception tickets with only three columns. The count shows missing PO numbers take 70% of exception time and handwritten POs only 17%. You show the table to two clerks, who agree: handwritten POs are annoying but missing POs mean chasing a buyer by email for days. The problem statement changes to focus on missing POs.
add_subtopics.code:
import csv, io
from collections import Counter

# Export of 90 days of AP exception tickets (masked sample, 10 rows shown)
data = """ticket_id,reason,minutes_to_resolve
T1,po_missing,35
T2,po_handwritten,20
T3,vat_mismatch,15
T4,po_missing,40
T5,duplicate_invoice,10
T6,po_missing,30
T7,po_handwritten,25
T8,po_missing,45
T9,vat_mismatch,12
T10,po_missing,38
"""
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)))
count = Counter(r["reason"] for r in rows)
minutes = Counter()
for r in rows:
    minutes[r["reason"]] += int(r["minutes_to_resolve"])

total = sum(minutes.values())
for reason, n in count.most_common():
    print(f"{reason:18} {n:2} tickets  {minutes[reason]:3} min  {minutes[reason]/total:.0%} of time")
# Output:
# po_missing          5 tickets  188 min  70% of time
# po_handwritten      2 tickets   45 min  17% of time
# vat_mismatch        2 tickets   27 min  10% of time
# duplicate_invoice   1 tickets   10 min  4% of time
checklist: Smallest sample requested: time window and columns named
Personal data masked, or you query inside the customer's environment
NDA and data processing agreement confirmed before data moves
Counts by reason and by time spent, not only by volume
Numbers shown back to users when they disagree with interviews
Storage location and deletion date written down

replace_subtopics.title: Preparing an interview guide
replace_subtopics.body:
An interview guide keeps you focused without turning the conversation into a script. It has three parts: what you want to learn (your goals), who you are talking to, and a short list of open questions grouped by theme.

Write 8 to 12 questions but expect to use about half. The guide is a safety net. The best material often comes from follow-ups like 'tell me more about that'.

Before each interview, read whatever you can find: the customer's org chart, recent tickets, a sample of the data. You will ask better questions and waste less of their time.

Write a separate, shorter guide for executives. A sponsor or director usually gives you 15 to 20 minutes, not 45, and cares about different things. Ask about the outcome they need, the budget and deadline, what their board or boss asks them about, and what would make them stop the project. Do not ask an executive to walk you through a screen; ask their team for that.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer wants to 'use AI for claims'. You schedule 45 minutes each with two claims handlers, a team lead and the claims operations director. Your goal is to learn where a claim waits the longest. Your guide has three themes: the daily workflow, the hardest recent claim, and how success is measured today. You also book 20 minutes with the claims operations director using the short executive guide below. She tells you the board tracks cost per claim and that the budget must be approved before the end of the quarter.

  - How will your boss or board judge whether it worked?

  - Who on your team should I shadow?

Background read: org chart, sample tickets or data
8 to 12 open questions grouped by theme
At least one 'last time you...' question
Recording or note-taker agreed with the interviewee
Closing question: who else should I talk to?

replace_subtopics.title: Open questions versus leading questions
replace_subtopics.body:
An open question lets the person answer in their own way, usually starting with what, how, tell me or walk me through. A leading question suggests the answer you want, for example 'Wouldn't it be faster if this were automated?'. People are polite, so they tend to agree with leading questions, and you learn nothing.

Ask about the past, not the future. 'Would you use a tool that...' produces guesses. 'Tell me about the last time you...' produces facts.

After asking, stay quiet. A pause of a few seconds often makes people add the most useful detail.

Sometimes the customer pushes back: "We already know what we want, just build it." Do not argue and do not refuse. Acknowledge the request, agree a short, fixed discovery time box (for example three days), and promise to come back with evidence. Then bring one data point that tests the ask. Often a single number changes the request, and the customer feels they discovered it, not that you overruled them. If the data supports their ask, you build it with more confidence.
replace_subtopics.example: At a hospital pharmacy you want to know if stock checks are painful. Leading: 'Stock checks must be a real pain, right?' Open: 'Walk me through yesterday's stock check.' The open question reveals that the pharmacist prints a report, walks the shelves and types counts back into a spreadsheet, which takes about an hour each morning. A support director says: "Just build us a chatbot." You reply: "Happy to. Can I spend three days looking at last quarter's tickets so the bot covers the right questions?" The ticket export shows 40% of contacts are password resets that a self-service reset link would solve without a chatbot. The director moves resets to the first release.

rows: Would an AI assistant help you?
Walk me through the last time you looked for an answer.
Is the search tool too slow?
What happens when you search for a policy?
You'd want this on mobile, right?
Where are you when you need this information?
Why does the approval step exist, as far as you know?
What have you already tried to fix this, and what did it cost?

replace_subtopics.title: Shadowing and capturing pain in their words
replace_subtopics.body:
Shadowing means sitting with a user, in person or on a screen share, and watching them do real work. People forget or skip steps when they describe their job. Watching shows the extra spreadsheet, the sticky note of passwords and the copy-paste between systems.

Write down pain as verbatim quotes, meaning the exact words the person used. 'I dread month-end' tells you more than your summary 'month-end is inefficient'. Quotes are also powerful later in a demo or a PRD.

Note timings and counts when you can: how many screens, how many minutes, how many times a day. These become your baseline, the 'before' number you will improve.

While you shadow, collect real input samples: 20 to 50 actual documents, emails or records the user handles, including the ugliest ones such as a handwritten PO, a blurry phone photo of a receipt or a scan that is upside down. Clean samples make any AI look good. The ugly ones tell you early whether the idea is feasible and what share of inputs will need a human. Ask permission first, take samples only through an approved channel, and mask personal data (names, addresses, bank details) before they leave the customer's systems.
replace_subtopics.example: You shadow an accounts payable clerk at a logistics company for an hour. She opens an emailed invoice PDF, retypes 14 fields into the ERP, then checks the purchase order in a second system. You time five invoices at about 6 minutes each and write down her quote: 'The worst part is when the PO number is handwritten.' Before you leave you ask the clerk for 30 recent invoices, including the five she calls 'the nightmares'. The AP lead approves, and the files are masked and placed in the customer's shared folder that you can access.

replace_subtopics.title: Writing the problem statement
replace_subtopics.body:
After the interviews, group your notes into themes, count how often each comes up, and pick the one with the most pain and the clearest path to improvement.

Then write a problem statement: who has the problem, what it is, how often or how much it costs, why it happens and how success will be measured. Keep it to one paragraph.

Share it with the sponsor and at least one user. If they say 'yes, that is it', you are ready to design. If they correct you, that is cheap now and expensive later.

A simple way to synthesise is affinity mapping. Write each observation or quote on its own sticky note (or a row in a spreadsheet). Group notes that say similar things into clusters, name each cluster, and count the notes in it. The biggest clusters, weighted by how much time or money they cost, are your candidate problems.

How many interviews are enough? Keep going until you reach saturation: the point where new interviews add no new themes, only more examples of old ones. For one team this often happens after 5 to 8 conversations.

Finally, turn the statement into an opportunity size, a rough value in hours or money. That number feeds the business case (see the roi concept).
replace_subtopics.example: After eight interviews and two shadowing sessions at the logistics company, the strongest theme is manual invoice entry. You write the statement below and the finance director agrees, adding that month-end is when it matters most. Your affinity map has 64 notes. The largest cluster, 'retyping invoice fields', has 21 notes; 'chasing missing POs' has 14. Interviews 7 and 8 added no new clusters, so you stop. Opportunity size: 1,500 invoices a month x 4 minutes saved (from about 6 down to 2) = 6,000 minutes = 100 hours a month.
replace_subtopics.code:
PROBLEM STATEMENT
Who:      Accounts payable clerks (6 people) at the logistics company
Problem:  Manually retype invoice fields from PDFs into the ERP
Size:     ~6 min per invoice, ~1,500 invoices a month (from our timing)
Why:      Invoices arrive as email PDFs in many layouts; no extraction
Impact:   Month-end backlog, late-payment fees, retyping errors
Success:  Median handling time under 2 min per invoice,
          field error rate at or below today's, within 8 weeks
Evidence: 8 interviews, 2 shadowing sessions, clerk quotes attached

OPPORTUNITY SIZE
1,500 invoices/month x 4 min saved = 6,000 min = 100 hours/month
(feeds the ROI model: 100 h x loaded hourly cost)

add_glossary: Triangulation
Checking what people say in interviews against a second source, such as system data, before you trust it.
Affinity mapping
Grouping observation notes into clusters by theme and counting them to find the biggest problems.
Saturation
The point in discovery when new interviews add no new themes.
Opportunity size
A rough estimate of the value of solving a problem, such as hours saved per month.
add_practice: Take any small export you can get (your own email folder counts or a public ticket dataset), count items by reason and by time, and write two sentences on whether the numbers agree with what people complain about most.

replace_subtopics.title: POC versus pilot versus production
replace_subtopics.body:
The three words are often mixed up, and the mix-up causes disappointment. A POC answers a feasibility question: can this approach work on their data at all, at a sensible cost? It usually uses historical or sample data, a small team and no connection to live systems. It ends with a readout and a go or no-go decision.

A pilot answers a value question: does it help real people in their daily work? It runs with a limited group of real users, real data and at least basic security and support, for weeks or months. It is usually paid. The arc lesson describes running a pilot well.

Production is the full, supported service under a contract, with service levels, monitoring and change control.

Say out loud which one you are running, and write it down. Many customers expect a POC to become the production system by adding users. It rarely can, because a POC skips security hardening, integration and support on purpose so it can move fast.

Sometimes the POC is a competitive bake-off: the customer runs the same test against two or three vendors and picks one. Ask early for the shared evaluation set, the scoring method, who scores and how ties are broken. If every vendor uses its own data or its own metric, the results cannot be compared and the decision falls back on the slickest demo. Offer to help design a fair test; customers usually welcome it.
replace_subtopics.example: A regional water company, Quarrymoor Water, asks for a 'pilot' of AI fault triage. On the first call the FDE learns they have no labelled data, no API access to the job system yet and no users identified. She proposes a four-week POC on historical reports first, with a paid pilot as the agreed next step if criteria are met. Quarrymoor later reveals two other vendors are also testing fault triage. The FDE asks for the same 300 labelled reports for all three, blind scoring by the same supervisors and the same cost-per-report calculation, and Quarrymoor agrees.

replace_subtopics.title: Written success criteria before you start
replace_subtopics.body:
The single most important POC document is one page of success criteria, agreed and signed before work starts. It turns 'let's see how it goes' into a test with a clear result.

Good criteria are measurable and tied to the customer's question. Each one names a metric, a baseline if one exists, a target, and how and by whom it is measured. The SMART criteria in the arc lesson apply here too. For AI POCs, agree the evaluation set early: who labels it, how many examples, and whether reviewers see the AI's answers blind.

Two lines are often forgotten. The first is the decision rule: what happens if the criteria are met, and what if they are not. Writing 'if met, a paid pilot starts in May' makes the commercial next step part of the agreement. The second is the list of non-goals, such as 'no integration with the live job system in the POC'.

Keep it to three to five criteria. More than that and the POC becomes a feature checklist instead of a test of the main question.

Remember that a small evaluation set gives an uncertain answer. If the AI scores 85% on 300 labelled reports, the true accuracy could reasonably be anywhere from about 81% to 89% (a 95% interval of roughly plus or minus 4 points). On 100 reports the band is about plus or minus 7 points. So a score of 84% against a target of 85% is not a clear failure, and the decision rule should say how you treat results that close to the line, for example 'within 2 points: extend the test set before deciding'.

A target like 'P1 recall 100%' also needs a minimum number of P1 (most urgent) cases. If the set has only 10 P1 reports and the AI catches all 10, the true miss rate could still be as high as about 30%. A handy rule of thumb, the rule of three, says that with zero misses in n cases the true miss rate could be up to about 3/n. Aim for at least 30 P1 cases, which caps it near 10%, and say so in the criteria.
replace_subtopics.example: Quarrymoor's sponsor first says success means 'the AI understands our faults'. The FDE turns this into four measurable criteria, with a 300-report labelled test set chosen by the maintenance planning lead. The sponsor also agrees in writing that meeting three of them leads to a paid pilot in the North region. The criteria sheet adds a line: 'Test set contains at least 40 P1 reports; results within 2 points of a target trigger 100 more labelled reports before the decision.'

Question the POC answers:
  Can AI triage of field fault reports cut time-to-assign for crews?

Scope: 1 region (North), 3 months of historical reports (about 9,000)
Time box: 4 weeks, 2 FDEs, 1 customer analyst at 20 percent

1  Correct fault category            n/a        >= 85%    300 labelled reports
2  Correct priority (P1-P4)          n/a        >= 90%    same set, P1 recall 100%
3  Time to assign (simulated)        47 min     <= 15 min replay of 2 weeks

replace_subtopics.title: Scoping: in, out and customer commitments
replace_subtopics.body:
Scope is what the POC will cover. Keep it narrow: one workflow, one team or region, one data source if possible. Every extra system you connect adds access requests and security reviews that can eat the whole time box.

Use fixed time, variable scope. The end date does not move; if something takes longer than expected, you drop lower-priority scope instead of extending. Rank scope items in advance so that choice is quick.

A POC also depends on the customer. Write down what they must provide and by when: sample data, system access, a named analyst's time, subject-matter experts to label examples, and a meeting slot for the readout. When a commitment slips, say so the same day and show what it costs in scope.

Watch for scope creep dressed as enthusiasm. 'Could it also do the invoices?' is a good sign for the future and belongs on a list for the pilot. Free POCs are the most likely to drift, which is one reason some vendors charge a small fee: it makes both sides take the dates seriously.

Agree how data is handled before any data moves. Four questions matter. First, paperwork: an NDA (non-disclosure agreement) and, if the data contains personal information, a DPA (data processing agreement) must be signed first. Second, location: does the POC run in the vendor's sandbox or inside the customer's own cloud tenant? Customer tenants are slower to set up but calm security teams. Third, minimisation: can you use masked data, where names and account numbers are replaced, or synthetic data, which is generated to look realistic but describes no real person? Fourth, the end: write a deletion date and how deletion will be confirmed in writing.
replace_subtopics.example: In week two, Quarrymoor's operations team asks whether the POC could also draft replies to customer complaints. The FDE thanks them, adds it to the 'pilot candidates' list in the shared document, and keeps the POC on fault triage. The readout later lists it as the second use case, which strengthens the case for the pilot. Quarrymoor's fault reports contain customer addresses and phone numbers. The POC scope says: NDA and DPA signed on day 0, POC runs in Quarrymoor's own cloud account, phone numbers and names masked by their analyst before loading, all copies deleted within 10 working days of the readout with a written confirmation.

Non-goals listed, including systems you will not connect
Data samples: which, how many, format and delivery date
Access: accounts, network, tools, with named owners and dates
Customer people: analyst and expert hours per week
Scope items ranked, so you know what to drop first
Readout date booked with the decision maker attending
What happens next if the criteria are met
NDA and, for personal data, DPA signed before data moves
Where the POC runs: vendor sandbox or customer tenant
Masked or synthetic data used wherever possible
Deletion date and written confirmation of deletion agreed

replace_subtopics.title: Answering RFP technical sections
replace_subtopics.body:
Large organisations and public bodies often buy through an RFP. The customer sends a long document of requirements and questions, and each vendor answers in a fixed format by a deadline. An RFI (request for information) is a lighter, earlier version. Security questionnaires, often hundreds of questions, frequently come alongside.

FDEs are asked to answer the technical parts: architecture, integration, deployment, security, data handling and support. Answer each requirement with a clear compliance level first, then a short explanation and evidence. The table shows common levels.

Be precise and honest. RFP answers are often attached to the contract, so an optimistic 'yes' becomes a promise. If the product does not do something, say so and describe the nearest alternative and whether it meets the need behind the question. Reuse approved answers from a library, but reread each one for this customer; products change and a stale answer is a risk.

Finally, read the questions for what they reveal. A block of questions about on-premises deployment and data residency tells you what the security team worries about, which is useful for the POC and the pilot too.

Security questionnaires often come in standard formats. SIG Lite (from Shared Assessments) and the CAIQ (the Cloud Security Alliance's Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire) are common. Many vendors keep pre-filled versions of these and a public trust center: a web page with security documents, certifications and sub-processor lists that buyers can read, sometimes after signing an NDA. Pointing to them saves days.

Buyers now add AI-specific questions. Expect these and have approved answers ready: Is our data used to train any model? How long are prompts and outputs kept, and is zero data retention available? Which model providers act as sub-processors (third parties that process our data)? In which region does inference, the model call itself, run? Can we turn AI features off? Answer only what your contracts and your model provider's terms actually say, and check with your security or legal team when unsure.
replace_subtopics.example: Quarrymoor's procurement team sends a 140-question RFP with the POC invitation. The FDE marks 118 answers as standard, 14 as configurable, 5 as roadmap without dates, and 3 as not supported, each with the nearest alternative. The evaluation panel later says the honest 'not supported' answers made the rest more credible.

replace_subtopics.title: Turning a POC into a signed deal
replace_subtopics.body:
A successful POC does not sign itself. Between a good readout and a signed contract sit a business case, a security review, procurement and legal. Each has its own owner and calendar, and a POC that ends without a plan for them often stalls for months.

The demo lesson covers running the readout itself. Around it, three habits help. First, confirm the decision maker and the budget early, ideally before the POC starts, so the readout goes to someone who can say yes. Second, keep a mutual action plan: a shared, dated list of every step to signature and go-live, with owners on both sides. It makes delays visible without blame. Third, give your sponsor what they need to sell it internally: a one-page summary with results against criteria, costs, risks and the recommended next step, in words their own leadership uses.

The FDE's role is technical credibility, not sales pressure. You make sure the results are honest, the production path is realistic and the security team's questions are answered quickly. When those are in place, the commercial conversation is much easier for everyone.

Build a mid-point checkpoint into every POC. Halfway through, review early results with the sponsor against the criteria and apply an agreed early-stop rule, for example 'if category accuracy is below 60% at the midpoint, we stop and write up findings'. This saves both sides weeks when the approach clearly will not work.

Treat a well-evidenced no-go as a good outcome. It saves the customer money and a failed rollout, and it builds trust you can use for the next use case. Write it up with the same care as a success: what was tested, what the numbers were, why it missed and what would have to change.
replace_subtopics.example: Quarrymoor's POC meets three of four criteria, missing the time-to-assign target at 19 minutes against 15, because assignments still waited for a supervisor's sign-off. The readout names the miss and the process fix. The mutual action plan below takes the pilot from readout to kick-off in four weeks, with the security review started before procurement instead of after it. At the week-2 checkpoint, category accuracy is 78%, above the 60% stop line, so the POC continues. In a different POC for invoice matching the same rule triggered at 45%, the team stopped, and the customer later came back with a better-labelled dataset.

add_glossary: Confidence interval
A range that likely contains the true value; small test sets give wide ranges.
Rule of three
With zero failures in n tests, the true failure rate could still be up to about 3/n.
Bake-off
A competitive POC where several vendors are tested on the same criteria.
Trust center
A vendor web page with security documents, certifications and sub-processor lists for buyers.
Sub-processor
A third party, such as a model provider, that processes customer data on the vendor's behalf.
Synthetic data
Generated data that looks realistic but describes no real person or transaction.
add_practice: Your POC scored 83% against an 85% target on 200 labelled items. Work out the rough margin (1.96 x sqrt(p(1-p)/n)) and write the decision-rule line you wish you had agreed before starting.

add_subtopics.title: Delivering bad news early
add_subtopics.body:
Bad news does not improve with age. The no-surprises rule says a sponsor should hear about a slip or a missed target from you, before they find it on a dashboard or hear it from their own team. An executive who learns about a problem from someone else stops trusting your status reports, even the green ones.

Tell them as soon as you are fairly sure, not when you are certain. A good bad-news message does four things. It owns the problem in plain words, without blaming the customer or another team. It gives the impact in business terms: what date, metric or team is affected. It gives a new date with an honest confidence level, such as 'high confidence' or 'depends on one open item'. And it offers two or three options with a recommendation, so the sponsor has something to decide instead of something to worry about.

Send it in writing the same day, and offer a short call if they want to talk it through. Writing creates a record and lets them forward it upward unchanged.

This subtopic covers the executive side. For the day-to-day craft of saying no and writing hard messages in chat and email, see the asyncwriting topic (Writing and async communication).
add_subtopics.example: At a logistics company, the go-live for an AI routing assistant was 14 May. On 2 May the FDE learns that the customer's map data feed will not be approved by their security team until 12 May. She emails the sponsor that afternoon: go-live moves to 21 May with high confidence, or 14 May with the assistant limited to two depots. The sponsor picks the limited launch and thanks her for the early warning.

replace_subtopics.title: Two tracks during an incident
replace_subtopics.body:
An incident is any event where the system stops doing what users need. During an incident you run two tracks in parallel. Track one is technical: find the cause and restore service. Track two is human: keep the people affected informed and calm.

New FDEs often drop track two because the technical problem feels more urgent. The result is silence, and silence makes executives assume the worst. A short message every hour or so, even when nothing has changed, keeps trust intact while you debug.

If your pod has two people available, split the tracks between them. One person debugs. The other writes updates, fields calls and keeps a timeline. When you are alone, set a timer so you remember to send updates.

Most teams sort incidents by severity level so everyone knows how fast to move. A common scale is SEV1 (the service is down or data is at risk for many users: updates every 30 to 60 minutes), SEV2 (a major feature is degraded: updates every 2 to 4 hours) and SEV3 (a minor issue with a workaround: an update each day). Name one incident lead who makes decisions and owns the timeline, so the customer knows who is in charge.

After the fix, the customer usually wants a customer-facing incident report. It differs from your internal blameless postmortem, which lists every technical detail and lesson. The customer report is shorter and plain: what happened, the impact on them, how it was fixed and what will prevent it happening again. Running incidents in full, with roles, war rooms and status pages, is covered in the incidents topic (Incidents and escalations in the field).
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims assistant slows from 2 seconds to 8 seconds per answer at 10:00. You post a holding note to the CIO at 10:20, start pulling logs, and find at 11:05 that a vendor API is rate limiting your calls (refusing requests because you sent too many). You switch to cached results as a workaround at 13:40. Between 10:20 and 13:40 the CIO received three short updates, so the escalation never grew. The insurer slowdown is declared a SEV2 at 10:15, with you as incident lead, so updates go out at least every 2 hours. On Wednesday the CIO gets a one-page incident report; the longer internal postmortem stays with your engineering team.

replace_subtopics.title: Listen and restate before you explain
replace_subtopics.body:
Active listening means showing the other person you understood them before you respond. The simplest technique is to restate their problem in their own business terms: 'So the claims team is falling behind and customers are waiting longer for answers. That is the priority.'

Restating does two things. It lowers the emotional temperature, because the executive feels heard. It also checks that you are solving the right problem. Sometimes the executive's real worry turns out to be a board meeting on Thursday, which changes what you should prioritise.

After restating, say three things: what you are doing now, when they will hear from you next, and who to call in the meantime. Avoid technical explanations at this stage. You do not know the cause yet, and guessing out loud creates promises you may have to take back.

Apologise for the impact, not for the cause. 'I am sorry your nurses could not see their shifts this morning' is honest and kind. Do not guess who is to blame, and do not talk about liability, refunds or SLA credits (money back promised in the service level agreement) on the call. You do not know the cause yet, and those are contract questions. Say that you will pass them to the account team, then do it the same day.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital's COO calls because nurses cannot see tomorrow's shift schedule in the new AI scheduling tool. You say: 'Nurses on three wards cannot see tomorrow's shifts, and that risks gaps in cover tonight. I am looking at it now with our engineer, and I will call you back by 15:00 with either a fix or a manual fallback.' You have not explained anything technical, and the COO knows exactly what happens next. The COO asks, 'Are we getting a credit for this?' You answer: 'That is a fair question. I will ask our account manager, Joe, to come back to you on the contract side today. My focus right now is getting your nurses their schedule.'

replace_subtopics.title: Answer first: pyramid principle and SCQA
replace_subtopics.body:
The pyramid principle, popularised by Barbara Minto, says to start with your main conclusion and then give the supporting points. Executives often read only the first two lines of a message, so those lines must carry the answer.

SCQA is a way to order the rest: Situation (what was happening), Complication (what went wrong), Question (what the reader wants to know) and Answer. In an incident update you usually put the Answer at the very top, then Situation, Complication, cause, prevention, and your ask.

Keep it to five to seven lines. Use plain words and numbers. End with one specific request, such as a 30-minute meeting with a named person, so the executive has something concrete to do.

The same answer-first habit applies to everyday async messages: put the ask and the deadline in the subject line, keep one topic per message, and move any decision made in chat into the recap email or decision log so it is not lost in a thread. The asyncwriting topic (Writing and async communication) covers these norms in depth.
replace_subtopics.example: The CIO receives this at 13:50: 'Fixed at 13:40, no data lost.' The next lines explain that about 1,100 claims took three times longer between 10:00 and 13:40, that a vendor began rate limiting, that caching and an alert are now in place, and that you would like 30 minutes with their vendor manager. The CIO forwards it to the board unchanged, which is the sign of a good update. A subject line such as 'Decision needed by Thu: add Exceptions report to go-live?' tells the reader what you need and by when before they open the message.

replace_subtopics.title: Storytelling in reviews and presentations
replace_subtopics.body:
Beyond incidents, you will present progress to executives in steering meetings and quarterly business reviews (QBRs), which are regular meetings where a vendor shows a customer the value delivered. The same answer-first rule applies at the level of a whole presentation.

A reliable structure has three parts. First, the result against the agreed success metric. Second, the story of how you got there, including one real user quote. Third, what comes next and the decision you need. Put the detail in an appendix so people can find it if they ask.

Rehearse the first 60 seconds. If the meeting is cut short, the executive should still leave knowing whether the project is working and what you need from them.

Pre-wire important meetings. A few days before a steering meeting, brief the key executive one to one: show them the main result and the decision you will ask for. Nobody should be surprised in the room, because surprised executives defend themselves instead of deciding. Pre-wiring also shows you objections early, while you can still answer them.

Sometimes two executives want different outcomes, for example the COO wants speed and the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) wants more security review. Do not pick a side yourself. Write both positions down fairly, with the trade-offs, and take the conflict to the executive sponsor, who owns the decision. Your job is to make the choice clear, not to make it.
replace_subtopics.example: For a retailer's demand forecasting pilot, your first slide says: 'Forecast error for fresh produce fell from 31% to 22% in 6 stores, cutting waste by an estimated 9 tonnes a month.' Slide two shows the store manager who now orders from the forecast. Slide three asks the COO to approve rollout to 40 more stores. Before the retailer's steering meeting, you walk the COO through the rollout slide in a 20-minute call. She asks about store staffing, so you add a line on it. When the finance director later pushes for a slower rollout, you present both views to the sponsor on one slide and let her decide.

add_subtopics.title: User-facing documentation
add_subtopics.body:
The SOW, PRD and design doc are for the project team. The people who use the system every day need different documents, written in their words. Four are standard.

An end-user quick-start is one page: what the tool is for, how to open it, the three most common tasks with screenshots, and who to ask for help. If it runs past one page, users will not read it.

An admin guide is for the customer staff who run the tool: adding users and roles, changing settings, re-indexing documents, reading the usage dashboard and what to do when something fails.

A FAQ of known limits tells users honestly what the tool does not do well, for example 'it does not read handwritten notes' or 'answers about policies older than 2024 may be missing'. Stating limits up front prevents surprise and builds trust.

Release notes, also called a changelog, list what changed in each version: new features, fixes and anything users must do differently. Date and number each version.

Decide before handover who owns each document. Usually the customer's admin or Center of Excellence owns the quick-start and FAQ, and the vendor owns release notes. A document with no owner goes out of date within months. Training and enablement materials are covered in the enablement topic (Customer enablement and the AI CoE).
add_subtopics.example: For the bank assistant, the FDE writes a one-page quick-start for branch advisors, a 6-page admin guide for the bank's IT team, a FAQ listing four known limits, and release notes starting at version 1.0. At handover the bank's knowledge manager takes ownership of the quick-start and FAQ.

add_subtopics.title: Architecture diagrams customers understand
add_subtopics.body:
Most customer reviewers look at the architecture diagram before they read a word of the design doc. A good diagram shows the right amount of detail for its reader.

The C4 model is a simple way to choose that level. It has four zoom levels. Level 1, context: your system as one box, the people who use it and the other systems it talks to. Level 2, containers: the separately deployed parts, such as the web app, the API, the database and the model provider. Level 3, components: the main parts inside one container. Level 4, code: classes and functions, which you rarely draw by hand. Executives and security teams usually need levels 1 and 2 only.

For each arrow, label what flows and how: 'policy text, HTTPS' or 'user questions, logged 30 days'. Security reviewers care most about where data crosses a boundary, so draw the customer's network or cloud account as a box around the parts inside it.

Draw diagrams as code where you can. Mermaid is a text format that tools such as GitHub, GitLab and many wikis render as a diagram. Because it is text, it lives in the repository next to the design doc, changes show up in code review, and it never goes stale in a forgotten slide.

add_subtopics.title: Runbooks and handover docs
add_subtopics.body:
A runbook is a step-by-step guide for operating the system when you are not there. It answers: when this alert fires or this symptom appears, what does it mean, how do I confirm it and what is the first safe action? The person reading it may be woken at 3 am and new to the system, so write short numbered steps with exact commands and links.

A good runbook entry has a fixed shape: the symptom or alert name, what it means, how to confirm it, first safe actions, when and to whom to escalate, and how to roll back. 'Safe' matters: the first steps should never make things worse, for example restarting a worker is safe, deleting a queue is not.

A handover doc sits above the runbooks. It lists everything the customer team needs to own the system: architecture diagram, environments and access, where the code lives, credentials and who holds them, scheduled jobs, monitoring dashboards, known issues, the runbook index and the support contacts. Walk through it live with the new owners and have them run one runbook entry themselves, a drill, before you leave.

Who answers which ticket after handover, the L1, L2 and L3 support split, and how hypercare ends are covered in the supportops topic (Support model, escalation and hypercare). The mechanics of alerts and on-call are in the observability topic.

replace_subtopics.title: The statement of work
replace_subtopics.body:
A SOW is usually attached to a master services agreement, the main contract between the two companies. The SOW covers one project: objectives, scope, deliverables, timeline, acceptance criteria, responsibilities on both sides, assumptions and fees.

Acceptance criteria are the most important part for an engineer. They are testable conditions the customer checks before signing off a deliverable. 'An AI assistant' is not testable. 'The assistant answers the agreed 100-question test set with at least 85% judged correct by the bank's reviewers' is.

Also list what is out of scope and what the customer must provide, such as data access by a certain date. Many delays come from customer dependencies that were never written down.

The SOW also sits under a commercial model. Under fixed price, the customer pays an agreed amount for the agreed scope, so every scope change needs a change request, and an overrun costs your company money. Under time and materials (T&M), the customer pays for hours worked, so the risk of overruns moves to the customer and the sponsor will watch hours closely. Milestone payments release money when a deliverable is accepted, which makes clear acceptance criteria even more important. As an FDE, check which model applies before you agree to 'just one more thing'. Pricing and services economics are covered in the psa topic (Professional services operations and PSA).

Read four clauses yourself, even though legal writes them. IP ownership: who owns the custom code, adapters and prompts you build, and can your company reuse them for other customers? Warranty or hypercare: how long after go-live you must fix defects for free (see the supportops topic). Deemed acceptance: many SOWs say a deliverable counts as accepted if the customer raises no written objection within, say, 10 business days. Data return and deletion: what happens to customer data, logs and test sets when the project ends, and by when.
replace_subtopics.example: For the bank project, the SOW lists three deliverables: a data connector to the product policy library, the assistant web app, and a two-week pilot in five branches. The bank must provide read access to the policy library by week 2. Integration with the core banking system is explicitly out of scope. The bank SOW is fixed price with three milestone payments. The IP clause says the bank owns its configuration and prompts while the vendor keeps the connector code, the warranty covers 30 days after go-live, deliverables are deemed accepted after 10 business days without objection, and all bank data is deleted within 30 days of the end date.

replace_subtopics.title: Keeping a decision log
replace_subtopics.body:
A decision log is a simple table, often in a shared doc, where each significant decision gets one row: date, decision, options considered, reason, who decided and any follow-up.

It answers the question 'why did we do it this way?' months later, when the original people may have moved on. It also stops the same debate from happening in every meeting.

Log decisions that change scope, architecture, cost or risk. Small coding choices do not need an entry.

When a decision changes the SOW, write a change request. It is a short, formal document the sponsor signs, and it becomes an amendment to the contract. It should state what changes, why, the impact on time, cost and risk, the options, who approves and the date.
replace_subtopics.example: Mid-project, the bank asks to add mortgage policies. You estimate two extra weeks. The sponsor decides to add mortgages and drop the branch manager dashboard to keep the date. You log it and raise a change request against the SOW. The mortgage decision above becomes change request CR-003, signed by the sponsor two days later.

replace_subtopics.title: The technical design doc
replace_subtopics.body:
A design doc explains how you will build the system and why you chose that way. It usually includes context, goals and non-goals, the proposed architecture, alternatives you considered, data and security, testing, rollout and open risks.

The 'alternatives considered' section is where reviewers learn the most. It shows you thought about other options and explains why you rejected them.

Share it early, as a draft, with the customer's engineers and security team. Their comments are much cheaper at this stage than after the code is written.

Agree the review workflow at the start. List the required approvers by name in the header, typically your tech lead, the customer's security architect and the data owner for each source. Reviewers leave comments; every comment is either resolved with a change or answered with a reason, and nothing is marked approved while a blocking comment is open. Use version numbers (v0.1 draft, v1.0 approved) and record the approval date in the doc. Keep the approved version in one agreed place, so a year later anyone can find exactly what security signed off.
replace_subtopics.example: For the bank assistant, the design doc proposes retrieval-augmented generation over the policy library, hosted in the bank's cloud account. It compares this with fine-tuning a model on the policies and rejects fine-tuning because policies change weekly and answers need citations. The bank design doc v0.3 gets 27 comments. The security architect marks two as blocking (log retention and admin access). Both are fixed in v0.4, and v1.0 is approved on 18 March with names and date in the header.

add_subtopics.title: Handling questions and objections
add_subtopics.body:
Questions are a good sign: people ask about things they care about. Handle them so they help the story instead of derailing it.

Keep a parking lot. When a question is off the path, such as a detailed pricing question in the middle of the workflow, say 'Good question, let me park it and come back at the end', and write it where everyone can see. Then really come back to it.

Say 'I don't know' when you do not know. Follow it with a date: 'I don't know how long we keep audit logs by default. I will confirm by Thursday.' A guessed answer that turns out wrong costs more trust than an honest gap.

Never promise roadmap dates. Features that are planned can slip or change. Say what exists today, and offer to connect them with the product team if a future feature matters to their decision.

Four AI objections come up in almost every demo. Prepare short, honest answers that you can back with evidence, and check them with your team so every FDE gives the same answer.
add_subtopics.example: During the claims demo, the head of IT asks whether the model will be trained on their claims. The FDE answers from the approved line in the table below, adds the link to the trust center, and parks a follow-up question about data residency for the end of the meeting, where she answers it.

rows: Sometimes it can. That is why each answer cites its source and a person approves before anything is sent. Here is our measured error rate on your test claims.
Your data stays in your region, is not used to train models under our contract, and access is logged. Our security documents are on the trust center.
Running cost is about X per claim at your volume; we will confirm it in the pilot and can set a monthly cap.
It removes retyping and searching so handlers spend time on decisions. How you use the saved time is your choice, and we can help plan it with HR.

replace_subtopics.title: Build the demo around the user's workflow
replace_subtopics.body:
Start from a real person and a real task you saw in discovery. Show the steps in the order that person does them, using realistic data, and ideally the customer's own data if you are allowed.

Pick one workflow and do it well. Showing every feature makes the audience work to figure out what matters.

Name the user out loud: 'This is Priya, a claims handler. It's Monday and she has 40 new claims.' The audience will follow Priya more easily than a list of screens.

Consider showing one AI mistake on purpose. Pick a realistic error, such as a blurry photo where the assistant reads the wrong amount, and show how the user spots it and corrects it in two clicks. A demo that shows the safety net builds more trust than a flawless run, because everyone in the room knows AI makes mistakes and wants to see what happens when it does.
replace_subtopics.example: For an insurer, you demo the assistant through one motor claim: Priya opens the claim, the assistant has already extracted the damage details from photos and the repair quote, flags a mismatch in the repair cost, and drafts the approval note. Three screens, one story. After the smooth motor claim, you open a second claim with a smudged repair quote. The assistant reads 1,850 as 7,850, the cost check flags it, and Priya fixes the figure before approving. The claims manager says this is the part that convinced her.
checklist: One named user from discovery
One workflow, shown in the user's real order
Realistic data, customer data only if approved
The key moment happens in the first half
Every screen shown earns its place in the story

replace_subtopics.title: Tailoring to executives and end users
replace_subtopics.body:
Executives have little time and care about outcomes, cost, risk and timing. Lead with the result, show one short workflow, then talk about what it would take to roll out.

End users care about whether it fits their daily work. They want to see their exact screens, how edge cases are handled and what happens when the AI is wrong. Give them more time in the product and ask for their feedback.

Often you run two versions of the same demo for the same customer, one per audience.

There is often a third audience: the customer's IT and security engineers. They frequently decide whether the system can go live at all. They want to see the architecture, where data flows and is stored, how users log in (single sign-on), what is logged and for how long, and how access is controlled. Give them a separate technical session with the architecture diagram and a look at real logs, not the executive story.
replace_subtopics.example: For the insurer's COO, you open with 'cost per claim could drop because handling time falls', show one claim in two minutes, then cover pilot plan and data security. For the claims handlers, you spend twenty minutes on real claims, including a blurry photo the assistant cannot read, and show how the handler corrects it. For the insurer's security team, you run a 45-minute session: the architecture diagram, a login through their identity provider, an audit log entry for one claim, and the data retention settings. They leave with a list of three questions for the design doc.

replace_subtopics.title: Handling live failures
replace_subtopics.body:
Live demos fail: the network drops, a model returns an odd answer, a login expires. Plan for this in advance so a failure costs you thirty seconds instead of the meeting.

Prepare a fallback for every live step: a screen recording of the same flow, cached responses you can switch to, or screenshots. Test the whole demo on the same machine and network you will use, shortly before the meeting.

When something breaks, name it in one calm sentence, switch to the fallback and continue the story. Follow up afterwards with the cause. Do not debug in front of the audience.

Language models add a special risk: non-determinism. The same prompt can give a different answer live than it did in rehearsal, even with nothing broken. Reduce the risk. Pin the exact model version (a dated snapshot, not an alias that can change underneath you). Lower the temperature, the setting that controls randomness, where the model supports it. Pre-warm the system by running the key steps a few minutes before the meeting, so caches are filled and cold starts are over. And keep a cached output for the key step, the one moment the story depends on, so you can switch to it if the live answer is odd.
replace_subtopics.example: Halfway through a demo to a hospital's operations director, the LLM call times out. You say: 'That call timed out, so let me show you the recording of the same step from this morning.' You play 40 seconds of video and carry on. That evening you email the director a short note: the cause was a rate limit on the demo account, now raised. In rehearsal the assistant wrote a crisp approval note; live, it adds an unexpected paragraph. Because the model version is pinned and the note is cached, you say 'The wording varies run to run; here is the note it produced this morning' and move on.

replace_subtopics.title: A 10-minute demo script
replace_subtopics.body:
Write the demo down as a script with timings. You do not need to read it aloud, but writing it forces you to cut and to decide what each minute is for.

A good default for ten minutes: one minute of context, two minutes of the before story, four minutes of the live workflow, one minute of the after and its number, and two minutes for the ask and questions.

Rehearse at least twice with a timer, once with a colleague acting as a skeptical executive.

Check your screen before you share it. Turn on do-not-disturb so chat pop-ups and email previews do not appear. Use a clean browser profile with only the demo tabs open and no bookmarks, history or autofill that could show another customer's name or data. Close anything confidential. Set the zoom to about 125 to 150 percent so people on small screens can read it, and share a single window rather than your whole desktop when you can.

Before the COO demo you switch to a browser profile called 'Demo only', close the chat app, set zoom to 150% and share just that window.

replace_subtopics.title: The build-it-where decision
replace_subtopics.body:
When a customer asks for something new, you have three places to put it. Configuration means settings the product already supports, such as a threshold or a list of approvers. An adapter is a small piece of code at the edge that connects the product to one customer's systems without changing the product itself. Core means the shared product code that every customer runs.

The default is configuration first, then an adapter, and core only with evidence. Evidence usually means two or more customers need something similar, and a general version fits where the product is heading.

Write down your reasoning each time. A short note ('config, because only Harbourline Freight needs it; revisit if a second customer asks') makes it easy to spot repetition later.

Promotion to core is not finished when the core feature ships. Every tenant still running the old adapter must be migrated to the new feature, tested, and then the adapter code deleted. Skip that last step and you keep paying for both: the core feature and a pile of old adapters doing the same job, which is exactly the sprawl you wanted to avoid. Put the migration and the deletion on the plan with dates and an owner.
replace_subtopics.example: A freight company asks for invoices over 10,000 euros from its EMEA team to need a second approver. The product already supports approval rules, so this is configuration. A month later a retailer asks the same thing, and a third customer asks for approval chains by region. Now there is repetition, so you bring the product team a proposal for regional approval chains in core. When regional approval chains ship in core, the freight company is moved over in the first week, the retailer the week after, and the old adapter is deleted from the repository with a short note in the registry.

replace_subtopics.title: Isolating one-offs with config and adapters
replace_subtopics.body:
Isolation means a customer-specific change cannot break anything else. Configuration does this naturally. Adapters do it by sitting between the customer's system and a clean interface the product already expects.

A good adapter has an owner (a named person), tests, and a record in a registry so people know it exists. Without those three things, adapters quietly become tech debt: code that costs more to maintain over time than it saved.

Never copy the core code into a customer branch to change one line. That is called forking, and it means every future product update has to be merged by hand into that customer's copy.

A third isolation tool is the per-tenant feature flag: a switch, stored in configuration, that turns a behaviour on for one customer without a separate code branch. The code for the new behaviour ships to everyone but runs only where the flag is on. This lets you try a change with one customer, and turn it off in seconds if it misbehaves.

Flags need cleanup. Each flag should have an owner and a removal date. Once the behaviour is on for everyone, or abandoned, delete the flag and the dead code path. Old flags multiply the combinations you have to test.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital exports patient appointments as a fixed-width text file instead of JSON. Rather than teaching the core scheduler to read that format, you write a 40-line adapter that converts the file into the standard appointment objects. The scheduler never knows the hospital is different. The hospital wants appointment reminders sent 48 hours ahead instead of 24. You add a flag `reminder_48h` with an owner and a removal date, turn it on for stmarys only, and after two other hospitals ask for it, make 48 hours a normal setting and delete the flag.

replace_subtopics.title: Process data as a moat
replace_subtopics.body:
Features are easy to copy. A competitor can watch a demo and build something similar in months. What they cannot copy is data they do not have.

Process data is the record of how work actually happens inside customers: which suggestions users accepted, which they corrected, what the correct answer turned out to be, and which exceptions came up. It is created as a side effect of people using your product in real workflows.

To make it useful, capture it deliberately. Log each model suggestion together with what the user did and the final outcome, in a consistent format. Respect the contract: customers must agree to how their data is used, often in anonymised or aggregated form.

Check the contract before you log anything for training. Many enterprise contracts forbid using one customer's data to improve models for other customers. The usual safe patterns are per-tenant opt-in (each customer agrees in writing, and the consent is stored with the data, as in the consent_scope field above), aggregation or anonymisation (removing names and details so records cannot be traced back), and training only within one tenant's own model. Also check your model provider's terms: some deployments run with zero data retention, where the provider keeps nothing, so prompts and outputs exist only in your own logs.

Data is also not the only moat, and on its own it is getting weaker: each new foundation model does more out of the box, so a pile of generic data buys less than it used to. Stronger moats in enterprise AI usually combine several things: switching costs from deep integration with the customer's systems, being embedded in daily workflows, a library of evaluation sets built with customers, and domain know-how in the team.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurance claims product suggests a damage category for each claim. When an adjuster changes 'minor collision' to 'total loss', the product logs the original suggestion, the correction, and the final payout. After a year across 12 insurers, the vendor has hundreds of thousands of expert-labelled corrections that no new entrant can buy. Before building the correction log, the claims vendor finds that 9 of its 12 insurers allow aggregate training, 2 allow training only on their own tenant, and 1 forbids any training use. The logging code reads each tenant's consent_scope and drops events that are not allowed.

add_subtopics.title: Retiring the old way and expanding
add_subtopics.body:
While the old way still works, many people will keep using it. The spreadsheet, the manual report or the old inbox is a safety blanket, and running both doubles the work, as the claims example in 'Why good tools still fail' shows. So adoption is not finished until the old way is retired, on purpose and on a date.

A decommission plan has five parts. A retirement date, agreed by the sponsor and announced early. A named owner who makes sure it happens. A read-only period, usually two to four weeks, where the old spreadsheet or report can still be opened but not edited, so people can look up history without drifting back. An archive: where old data will live afterwards and who can reach it. And a check that nothing else depended on it, for example another team's monthly report that quietly reads the old spreadsheet.

Once one team's workflow is proven and the old way is gone, you have the best evidence you will ever get: real numbers from real users. That is the moment to take the workflow to the next team, site or use case, reusing the champions, training and communication plan you already have. From the FDE side this is 'land and expand': land one team, prove it, expand. How the account team turns this into renewals and a second use case is covered in the expansion topic (Renewal, value realisation and expansion).
add_subtopics.example: At the distribution company, the old order-error spreadsheet becomes read-only on 30 March and is archived on 27 April, with the operations director as owner. The FDE finds that the finance team's month-end report reads that spreadsheet and moves it to the new tool's export first. In May the same order-check workflow, with two of the original champions as trainers, goes live at the second warehouse.

replace_subtopics.title: Handling resistance
replace_subtopics.body:
Resistance is any behavior that slows the change: complaints, workarounds, quiet non-use. It usually has a reason. The tool may add work, threaten someone's status or expertise, or have failed them once in front of a customer.

One widely used model, Prosci's ADKAR, says a person needs Awareness of why, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how, Ability to do it in practice, and Reinforcement so it lasts. Asking which of these is missing helps you pick the right fix: more explanation, a better reason, training, practice or follow-up.

Listen first. Ask the resistant person to show you where the tool gets in the way. Some complaints reveal real bugs. When the concern is about jobs or status, be honest about what you know, and bring the sponsor in for decisions you cannot make.

Watch for the opposite problem too: over-trust, also called automation bias. This is when users accept almost every suggestion without really checking, because the tool is usually right and checking takes effort. It looks like perfect adoption, but errors slip through unseen. Track the acceptance rate (suggestions accepted unchanged), the edit rate and the rejection rate. If users accept 98% of suggestions while your evaluation says the model is wrong about 5% of the time, some errors are being passed on. Audit a random sample each week, show users real examples of errors caught, and keep the review step meaningful, for example by asking them to confirm the one field that matters most.
replace_subtopics.example: A senior underwriter refused to use a risk-scoring assistant and told colleagues it was 'a black box'. The FDE sat with her for an hour. She showed two cases where the score ignored a clause she always checks. The team added that clause to the model's inputs and showed the reasoning for each score. She later became the team's champion. The underwriting team, once won over, accepted 392 of 400 risk scores unchanged in one month. A 40-case audit found two scores that missed an exclusion clause. The FDE shared both cases in the next team meeting and added a required tick box for that clause.

rejected = 2
print(f"Accepted unchanged: {accepted_unchanged/suggestions:.1%}")
print(f"Edited: {edited/suggestions:.1%}  Rejected: {rejected/suggestions:.1%}")
# Audit a random sample: if the model's real error rate is 5%,
# 98% unchanged acceptance means some errors are slipping through.
# Output:
# Accepted unchanged: 98.0%
# Edited: 1.5%  Rejected: 0.5%
checklist: Ask the person to show you, on screen, where it gets in the way
Identify which ADKAR element is missing
Separate real product gaps from habit or fear
Fix and tell them what changed because of their feedback
Bring the sponsor in for policy or job questions
