replace_subtopics.title: Measuring adoption
replace_subtopics.body:
Adoption needs numbers, the same as model accuracy. Three levels are useful. Breadth is the share of intended users who used the tool in a period, for example weekly active users divided by licensed users. Depth is the share of the relevant work that goes through the tool. Outcome is the business number the project was meant to move, such as handle time.

Logins alone mislead: people can log in and then do the work elsewhere. Depth catches that. Collect usage events from the start, since adding them later means you have no baseline.

Look at the data by team and by person. A low average often hides one team at 90 percent and another at 5 percent, and the fixes differ.

One week of breadth can hide a slow drop-off. Two more measures catch it. A retention cohort follows one group over time: of the users who were active in week 1, how many are still active in week 2, 3 and 4? A falling line means people tried the tool and stopped. Stickiness is average daily active users divided by weekly active users (DAU/WAU). If it is high, people use the tool most days; if it is low, they use it only now and then. For a tool meant for daily work, a low stickiness is a warning even when breadth looks fine.
replace_subtopics.example: A support tool has 6 licensed agents. In one week, 3 of them used it at least once (breadth 50 percent), and 4 of the 8 relevant tasks were done in the tool (depth 50 percent). The three non-users get a short conversation with their champion before the next weekly review. Five handlers used the tool in week 1, but only two of them were still active in week 4, a 40% retention. The two who stayed used it on most days (stickiness 70%), so the FDE interviews the three who stopped.
replace_subtopics.code:
from datetime import date

# One row per time a user did the target task: (user, day, done_with_tool?)
events = [
    ("ana", date(2026, 3, 2), True),  ("ana", date(2026, 3, 3), True),
    ("ben", date(2026, 3, 2), False), ("ben", date(2026, 3, 4), True),
    ("cara", date(2026, 3, 3), True), ("dev", date(2026, 3, 5), False),
    ("eli", date(2026, 3, 5), False), ("eli", date(2026, 3, 6), False),
]
licensed_users = ["ana", "ben", "cara", "dev", "eli", "fay"]

active = {u for u, d, used in events if used}             # used the tool at least once
reach = len(active) / len(licensed_users)                  # breadth: who uses it
tasks = [used for _, _, used in events]
depth = sum(tasks) / len(tasks)                            # depth: share of tasks done in the tool
not_started = [u for u in licensed_users if u not in active]

print(f"Weekly active: {len(active)}/{len(licensed_users)} = {reach:.0%}")
print(f"Tasks done in tool: {sum(tasks)}/{len(tasks)} = {depth:.0%}")
print("Follow up with:", not_started)
# Weekly active: 3/6 = 50%
# Tasks done in tool: 4/8 = 50%
# Follow up with: ['dev', 'eli', 'fay']

# Retention cohort: of the users active in week 1, who is still active later?
weekly_active = {
    1: {"ana", "ben", "cara", "dev", "eli"},
    2: {"ana", "ben", "cara", "eli"},
    3: {"ana", "cara", "eli"},
    4: {"ana", "cara"},
}
cohort = weekly_active[1]
for week, users in weekly_active.items():
    kept = len(cohort & users)
    print(f"Week {week}: {kept}/{len(cohort)} of the week-1 cohort active = {kept/len(cohort):.0%}")

# Stickiness: average daily active users / weekly active users
daily_active_counts = [2, 1, 1, 2, 1]      # Mon-Fri of week 4 (never above WAU)
wau = len(weekly_active[4])
dau = sum(daily_active_counts) / len(daily_active_counts)
print(f"Stickiness (DAU/WAU) in week 4: {dau:.1f}/{wau} = {dau/wau:.0%}")
# Output:
# Week 1: 5/5 of the week-1 cohort active = 100%
# Week 2: 4/5 of the week-1 cohort active = 80%
# Week 3: 3/5 of the week-1 cohort active = 60%
# Week 4: 2/5 of the week-1 cohort active = 40%
# Stickiness (DAU/WAU) in week 4: 1.4/2 = 70%

replace_subtopics.title: Communication plans
replace_subtopics.body:
A communication plan lists who needs to hear what, from whom, when, and through which channel. It prevents surprises, which are a major source of resistance.

Every message should answer the user's questions: what is changing, why, what it means for me, when, and where to get help. The sender matters. People listen to their own manager more than to a project email.

Plan several touches: an early heads-up, a go-live message, and follow-ups that share early results and fixes. Sharing 'you told us X, we changed Y' shows that feedback works and encourages more of it.

In some countries, workers' representatives must be involved before the rollout. In Germany, for example, a works council (Betriebsrat) has a right to be consulted on, and to agree to, technical tools that can monitor employee behaviour or performance, and usage logs of an AI tool can count. Similar rules exist elsewhere in Europe, and unions may have agreements too. Ask the customer's HR team early whether this applies. Involving them late can stop a go-live completely.
replace_subtopics.example: Two weeks before go-live at a distribution company, the operations director told team leads in their weekly meeting why the new order-check tool was coming. One week before, each team lead sent a short email to their team. On go-live day the champions posted in the team chat. Three weeks after, the director shared that order errors had dropped and listed two fixes that came from user feedback. Before the German warehouse rollout, HR tells the FDE that the works council must approve the tool because it logs which employee handled each order. The FDE prepares a one-page summary of what is logged, who can see it and how long it is kept, and approval comes three weeks later.

replace_subtopics.title: Training plans that stick
replace_subtopics.body:
Training works best when it is about the user's own tasks, uses realistic data, and happens close to when they will need it. People forget most of a demo within days if they do not practice.

Split training by role. A manager needs to read the dashboard and know what to expect from the team. A daily user needs to do their three most common tasks and know what to do when the tool is wrong.

Keep training short, add a one-page quick reference, and plan for new starters. A recording of a live session is useful as a backup, but hands-on practice is what builds confidence.

Training is not a single event. Plan ongoing support for at least the first month: weekly office hours where anyone can drop in with questions, short in-app tips on the screens where people get stuck, and a one-click feedback button that feeds the champion issue log. Each channel shows users that help is easy to find. For the broader programme of enablement, prompt libraries and the Center of Excellence, see the enablement topic (Customer enablement and the AI CoE).
replace_subtopics.example: For an insurer's claims summarizer, the FDE planned a 45-minute hands-on session per team of 10 handlers, held two days before their go-live. Each handler summarized three real past claims, compared them to the file, and practiced flagging a wrong summary. Team leads got a separate 20-minute session on the quality dashboard. For the claims summarizer, the FDE runs 30-minute office hours every Tuesday for four weeks and adds a 'Was this summary useful?' button. Most feedback in week 1 is about one confusing label, which is renamed by week 2.

Uses the user's real tasks and realistic data
Held within a few days of go-live
One-page quick reference handed out
Users practice what to do when the tool is wrong
Plan for new starters written down
Office hours, in-app tips and a feedback button planned for the first month

replace_subtopics.title: Agile and sprints in practice
replace_subtopics.body:
Agile means delivering in small, working increments and using feedback to decide what comes next. Scrum is a popular agile framework built around sprints and a few regular meetings, sometimes called ceremonies.

A sprint starts with planning, where the team picks work that fits. Each day a short standup covers progress and blockers. The sprint ends with a review, where working software is demoed, and a retrospective, where the team improves its own process.

FDE teams usually keep the rhythm and drop the heavy parts. A two-person team may skip formal story points but still plan every two weeks, demo to the customer at the end of each sprint and write down blockers daily.

Many FDE teams use Kanban instead of sprints. Kanban is a continuous flow: there are no fixed two-week boxes; work items move across a board with columns such as To do, In progress, Waiting on customer, In review and Done. The key rule is a WIP limit (work in progress limit): for example, at most three items in In progress at once. When the column is full, you finish something before starting something new. This suits FDE work well, because a lot of time is spent waiting on the customer and priorities change often. A 'Waiting on customer' column makes those blockers visible at a glance.

Many teams mix the two: a Kanban board for daily flow plus a demo to the customer every two weeks. Common tools are Jira, Linear and GitHub Projects; the customer may insist on their own, and it is usually easier to use theirs.
replace_subtopics.example: A two-person FDE team runs a six-week pilot at a regional insurer, split into three two-week sprints. Sprint 1 ends with a demo of claims summaries on 50 historical claims. Sprint 2 adds the handler review screen. Sprint 3 runs live with one team of eight handlers and ends with a results readout to the sponsor. A solo FDE supporting three small workflows at a logistics company uses a Kanban board in the customer's Jira with a WIP limit of 2 and a 'Waiting on customer' column. Every Friday she demos whatever reached Done that week.

replace_subtopics.title: Backlog and user stories
replace_subtopics.body:
The backlog is the single ordered list of all the work the team might do. The top items are small and well understood. Items further down can be rough ideas.

A user story describes a need from the user's point of view: As a [type of user], I want [something], so that [benefit]. It keeps the team focused on the person and the reason, which helps when you need to cut scope.

Acceptance criteria are the testable conditions that make a story done. A common format is Given (the situation), When (the action), Then (the expected result). A story that is too big to finish in one sprint gets split, for example by user type or by one path through the workflow.

Acceptance criteria belong to one story. The definition of done (DoD) is a checklist the team applies to every story, so 'done' means the same thing each time. For an AI project a typical DoD is: code reviewed, automated tests pass, the evaluation set still meets its thresholds (no drop in quality), deployed to the staging environment, and docs or release notes updated. A story that meets its acceptance criteria but fails the DoD is not done.
replace_subtopics.example: At an insurer, the story 'claims summaries' is too big. It is split into: show a summary for a single claim, let the handler flag a wrong summary, and show summaries for all claims in the handler's queue. The first story is done when a handler opens a claim and sees a summary within five seconds, with each fact linked to its source document. CLM-12 meets all its acceptance criteria on Tuesday, but the evaluation run shows summary accuracy fell from 91% to 86%. By the team's DoD it is not done, so the fix goes in before it is demoed.

replace_subtopics.title: The weekly status report
replace_subtopics.body:
A weekly status report tells the sponsor and stakeholders where the project stands in under two minutes of reading. It uses RAG status: red means the goal or date is at risk without help, amber means there is a problem the team is handling, green means on track.

A good report includes the overall color with one reason, what was done this week, what is planned next week, the top risks and issues, and a short list of asks with owners and dates. The asks section is the most useful part, because it turns the report into action.

Be honest about color. Moving to amber early, with a plan, builds trust. Staying green until the last week and then jumping to red destroys it.

Sponsors also want to see the dates that matter and what moves them. A milestone plan lists the key dates, such as data access, first demo, live start and readout, with the dependencies between them. The critical path is the chain of tasks where any delay moves the final date. Tasks off the critical path have slack (spare time) and can slip a little without harm. Show the sponsor which dependency sits on the critical path, so they know which ask really matters.

A note on names: RAG status here means red, amber, green. It has nothing to do with RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, the AI technique in other lessons of this atlas. In a status report for an AI project, spell out 'RAG status (red/amber/green)' once to avoid confusion.
replace_subtopics.example: In week 3 of the claims pilot, the model is ready but only 3 of 8 handlers have accounts. The FDE marks the project amber, explains that live use will start two days late unless accounts are created by Wednesday, and names the IAM team lead as the owner of that ask. In the claims pilot, the service account (D-3) sits on the critical path: every day it is late moves the readout a day. Handler training has four days of slack, so a two-day slip there does not move the readout. The sponsor chases the IAM team, not the training booking.

add_subtopics.title: Tracking realised value after go-live
add_subtopics.body:
A business case is a forecast. After go-live, the customer will ask whether the forecast came true, usually at the quarterly business review and certainly before renewal. Track realised value, the value actually delivered, from the first month.

Each month, put the forecast and the actual side by side, using the same formula as the case: measured adoption times measured saving times volume. Measure, do not re-estimate.

Then deal with attribution: how much of the change was caused by the tool? Handling times can fall for other reasons, such as a quiet season or a new process. The strongest method is a control group, a similar team that does not have the tool yet, for example a team scheduled for a later rollout wave. Subtract its change from the live teams' change. If no control group is possible, use a before and after comparison over the same season and say plainly that other factors may be mixed in.

When actuals differ from the forecast, update the case and explain why, for example slower adoption in month 1. A case that is updated honestly keeps its credibility. The account team uses these numbers in QBRs, success plans and the renewal conversation; that side is covered in the expansion topic (Renewal, value realisation and expansion).
add_subtopics.example: The claims summarizer went live in April. A fourth claims team, scheduled for the second wave, acts as the control group. Realised hours reach 58% of the forecast in April because adoption started at 55%, then 96% by June. The FDE adds these three months to the case, and the account manager puts the June figure on the first slide of the QBR.

# Realised value: forecast vs actual, with a control group
forecast_hours_per_month = 11_592 / 12          # from the business case
users, weeks_per_month = 120, 46 / 12
months = {
    # month: (measured adoption, hours/user/week change in live teams,
    #         same measure in a control team that does not have the tool yet)
    "Apr": (0.55, 2.4, 0.2),
    "May": (0.68, 2.8, 0.1),
    "Jun": (0.72, 3.1, 0.3),
}
for m, (adoption, treated, control) in months.items():
    net_saving = treated - control              # remove what changed anyway
    actual = users * adoption * net_saving * weeks_per_month
    print(f"{m}: actual {actual:,.0f} h vs forecast {forecast_hours_per_month:,.0f} h"
          f" = {actual / forecast_hours_per_month:.0%}")

# Apr: actual 557 h vs forecast 966 h = 58%
# May: actual 845 h vs forecast 966 h = 87%
# Jun: actual 927 h vs forecast 966 h = 96%

replace_subtopics.title: What a business case contains
replace_subtopics.body:
A business case answers five questions: what problem costs money today, what the solution changes, what it costs, what the return is, and what the risks are. It ends with a clear ask, such as funding for a rollout to three more teams.

Keep it short. One page of text plus a one-page calculation is enough for most decisions. Every number should have a source: the customer's data, a pilot measurement, or a clearly labeled assumption.

Write the assumptions in a separate list. It makes the case easy to challenge and easy to update when the pilot produces real measurements.

Compare the project against its alternatives, not only against doing nothing at zero cost. A CFO will ask 'compared with what?'. Show at least three options: do nothing (and what that costs as volume grows), a non-AI fix (such as a better search in the document store, a template, or one more contractor in peak season), and the AI solution. Sometimes the non-AI fix wins on cost and risk; saying so builds trust. When the AI solution wins, the comparison shows why.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims team of 120 handlers spends a large share of the day reading claim documents. A pilot of an AI summarizer suggests about 3 hours saved per handler per week. The business case states the baseline, the measured saving, the rollout cost, the running cost, the return, the risks and a request to fund rollout to all claims teams. For the claims team, the options are: do nothing (backlog grows about 8% a year, peak contractors cost more each year), improve document search (cheaper, saves about 1 hour per handler per week in a quick test) or the AI summarizer (about 3 hours). The case shows all three and recommends the summarizer, with better search as a cheaper fallback.

replace_subtopics.title: Estimating value from a baseline
replace_subtopics.body:
Value starts with a baseline, the measured state before the change: how many times the task happens, how long it takes, how often it goes wrong, and what that costs. Get these from the customer's systems where possible, since people's estimates of their own time are often off.

The basic formula is volume times improvement per unit times adoption times cost per unit. Adoption is the share of the work that will actually go through the new tool. The cost per hour should be the loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits, taxes and overheads, which finance teams can provide.

Separate hard savings from soft ones. Hard savings reduce spending, such as less overtime or fewer contractors. Soft savings free up capacity or improve quality. Both matter, but a CFO will weigh them differently.

Time is not the only source of value. Quality and risk often matter as much. Count the errors the tool prevents and multiply by the cost of one error: rework, overpayments, penalties, refunds or complaint handling. Add avoided incidents where there is evidence, for example a missed fraud flag or a regulatory breach, but label these carefully because they are rare and hard to predict.
replace_subtopics.example: For the insurer: 120 handlers x 70 percent adoption x 3 hours saved per week x 46 working weeks = 11,592 hours a year. At a loaded cost of 55 per hour, that is 637,560 per year of freed capacity. If the team currently pays for contractors during peak season, the part that replaces contractor spend is a hard saving; the rest is capacity. The insurer's audit sample shows 4% of claims are paid wrongly or reworked. In the pilot the rate fell to 2.5%. At 60,000 claims a year and about 180 per error, that is 162,000 a year of quality value on top of the time saved.

adoption       = 0.70     # share of work done with the tool

hours_per_year = users * adoption * hours_saved * weeks
value          = hours_per_year * hourly_cost
print(f"{hours_per_year:,.0f} hours/year, value {value:,.0f}")
# 11,592 hours/year, value 637,560

replace_subtopics.title: ROI, payback and NPV
replace_subtopics.body:
ROI over a period is total value minus total cost, divided by total cost. It tells you how much you get back per unit spent. Always say the time period, since an ROI over three years is not comparable with one over one year.

Payback period is the upfront cost divided by the net benefit per month. A short payback reduces risk, because the project earns back its money before much can change.

NPV, net present value, adds up future net benefits after discounting them, because money next year is worth less than money today. The discount rate, often around 8 to 12 percent, comes from the customer's finance team. A positive NPV means the project creates value at that rate. The calculator below keeps it simple and assumes a flat benefit each year; a real case often adds a ramp-up in the first months.

Many CFOs also ask for IRR, internal rate of return. It is the discount rate at which the NPV becomes exactly zero. Put simply, it is the yearly return the project earns on its money. Finance compares it with a hurdle rate, the minimum return the company expects from any investment (often 10 to 15 percent). A project whose IRR is well above the hurdle rate is attractive. IRR has no simple formula, so spreadsheets (the IRR function) and code find it by trying rates until the NPV reaches zero.
replace_subtopics.example: With the insurer's numbers, annual value is 637,560 and annual net benefit after running costs is 483,560. The 3-year ROI is 198 percent, the payback is about 4.5 months, and the NPV at 10 percent is 1,022,542. The summarizer's cash flows are -180,000 today and 483,560 at the end of each of three years. Its IRR is about 263%, far above a 12% hurdle rate. A slower project costing 600,000 that returns 250,000 a year has an IRR of about 12%, only just at the hurdle.
replace_subtopics.code:
def business_case(users, hours_saved_per_week, adoption, hourly_cost,
                  build_cost, annual_run_cost, years=3, weeks_per_year=46,
                  discount_rate=0.10):
    # Value: hours saved by the people who actually use the tool, priced at loaded cost
    annual_value = users * adoption * hours_saved_per_week * weeks_per_year * hourly_cost
    annual_net = annual_value - annual_run_cost          # benefit after running costs
    total_cost = build_cost + annual_run_cost * years
    total_value = annual_value * years
    roi = (total_value - total_cost) / total_cost          # return per 1 unit spent
    payback_months = build_cost / (annual_net / 12) if annual_net > 0 else float("inf")
    npv = -build_cost + sum(annual_net / (1 + discount_rate) ** t for t in range(1, years + 1))
    return {"annual_value": annual_value, "annual_net": annual_net,
            "roi": roi, "payback_months": payback_months, "npv": npv}

case = business_case(users=120, hours_saved_per_week=3, adoption=0.70,
                     hourly_cost=55, build_cost=180_000, annual_run_cost=154_000)
for k, v in case.items():
    print(f"{k:15} {v:,.2f}")

# Output
# annual_value    637,560.00
# annual_net      483,560.00
# roi             1.98
# payback_months  4.47
# npv             1,022,542.15

def npv_at(rate, flows):
    """flows[0] is today (year 0), flows[1] is end of year 1, ..."""
    return sum(f / (1 + rate) ** t for t, f in enumerate(flows))

def irr(flows, lo=-0.99, hi=10.0):
    """Find the rate where NPV = 0 by bisection (flows start negative)."""
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if npv_at(mid, flows) > 0:
            lo = mid          # still positive: the rate can go higher
        else:
            hi = mid
    return (lo + hi) / 2

flows = [-180_000, 483_560, 483_560, 483_560]    # build cost, then 3 years of net benefit
print(f"NPV at 10%: {npv_at(0.10, flows):,.0f}")
print(f"IRR: {irr(flows):.0%}")

# A slower case: bigger build, smaller benefit
slow = [-600_000, 250_000, 250_000, 250_000]
print(f"Slow case IRR: {irr(slow):.1%}")
# Output:
# NPV at 10%: 1,022,542
# IRR: 263%
# Slow case IRR: 12.0%

replace_subtopics.title: The full cost of an AI system
replace_subtopics.body:
Costs come in two kinds. One-time costs happen once, such as building, integrating and the initial security review. Recurring costs repeat every year, such as model or API usage, hosting, monitoring and the people who maintain the system.

AI systems have costs that normal software often does not. LLM usage is priced per token and grows with volume and prompt size. Evaluation and monitoring need ongoing work because model behavior can change when you update prompts or models. Someone has to review flagged outputs.

Include the customer's own internal costs too: their staff time for data access, testing and training. Leaving these out makes the case look better on paper and damages trust when the CFO notices.

Do not just state the LLM line; derive it, so anyone can check it and update it when volume or prices change. The formula is volume times tokens per item times price per token, done separately for input tokens (what the model reads) and output tokens (what it writes), because output usually costs more. The llmcost topic covers this method in depth, including caching and batch discounts.

TCO, total cost of ownership, is the name finance teams use for the full cost picture over the life of the system: one-time plus recurring costs, including the customer's own staff time. When a CFO asks for TCO, they mean this whole table over the case's horizon, not only the licence or API bill.
replace_subtopics.example: For the claims summarizer, the one-time build is 180,000, covering integration with the document store, the review screen, evaluation and security review. The recurring cost is 154,000 a year: 60,000 of LLM API usage for about 400,000 documents, 24,000 of hosting and monitoring, and 70,000 for half a full-time engineer to maintain prompts, evals and integrations. The 60,000 LLM line comes from: 400,000 documents a year, each about 35 pages or roughly 45,000 input tokens including instructions, plus about 1,000 output tokens for the summary and extracted fields. At an assumed 3 per million input tokens and 15 per million output tokens, that is 54,000 plus 6,000, so 60,000 a year. If the claim volume grows 20%, so does this line.
replace_subtopics.code:
LLM usage line (assumed prices; check the provider's current price list)
Input : 400,000 docs x 45,000 tokens = 18,000,000,000 tokens
        18,000 million x 3 per million  = 54,000
Output: 400,000 docs x 1,000 tokens  = 400,000,000 tokens
        400 million x 15 per million    = 6,000
Total : 60,000 per year

TCO over 3 years = 180,000 build + 3 x 154,000 run = 642,000
                   (plus customer staff time, listed separately)

add_glossary: Realised value
The value actually delivered after go-live, measured against the forecast in the business case.
Control group
A similar team without the tool, used to separate the tool's effect from other changes.
Attribution
Deciding how much of a measured change was caused by the project.
IRR
Internal rate of return: the discount rate at which a project's NPV is exactly zero.
Hurdle rate
The minimum return a company expects before it funds an investment.

Derive the LLM cost line of a case from volume x tokens x price, and write how you would track realised value monthly with a control group.

replace_subtopics.title: Weeks 1-2: find the pain and the baseline
replace_subtopics.body:
Scoping starts with discovery: interviewing the people who do the work and the leaders who pay for it. You map the workflow step by step, note which systems hold the data, and learn who makes decisions.

The most important output of discovery is a baseline, which is a measured number describing how things work today. Without a baseline you cannot prove improvement later. Get it from the customer's own systems where possible, because they will trust their own data.

Start data access requests on day one. In large companies, getting access to a database can take weeks, and it often becomes the critical path (the chain of tasks that sets the earliest finish date).

The engagement opens with a kick-off meeting, usually 60 to 90 minutes with the sponsor, the team lead of the pilot users, customer IT and your pod. A simple agenda: introductions and roles; the problem in the sponsor's words; a read-back of the draft success criteria, where you say them aloud and ask 'is this what you will judge us on?'; the 12-week plan; the dependency list; and how you will communicate (weekly demo, status report, shared channel).

Agree a RACI chart (who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed) for the main activities, so it is clear who approves data access and who signs off results. The dependency list names everything you need from the customer, with an owner and a date: accounts, data extracts, a test environment, time with users. Send notes with decisions and owners the same day. The pod topic covers RACI in more detail, and the asyncwriting topic covers writing clear follow-up notes.
replace_subtopics.example: At a motor insurer, handlers say triage is slow. You pull timestamps from the claims system and find the median time from 'claim received' to 'claim triaged' is 4.1 hours over the last 90 days, and 6.8 hours on Mondays. That number becomes the baseline for the whole engagement. At the kick-off with the insurer, you read back 'cut median motor triage time from about 4 hours to 1 hour by week 10'. The claims director corrects you: she cares about the p90 as well, because the slowest claims cause complaints. You add p90 to the criteria before anyone builds anything.
replace_subtopics.code:
-- Baseline: median and p90 time to triage, last 90 days (PostgreSQL)
SELECT
  team,
  COUNT(*) AS claims,
  percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
    ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600
  ) AS median_hours,
  percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (
    ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600
  ) AS p90_hours
FROM claims
WHERE received_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
  AND triaged_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY median_hours DESC;

KICK-OFF AGENDA (75 min)
 1. Introductions and roles                                 10 min
 2. The problem, in the sponsor's words                      10 min
 3. Read-back of success criteria: 'Is this how you will     15 min
    judge us?'
 4. 12-week plan and phase gates                            10 min
 5. Dependency list: owner and date for each                 15 min
    D-1 Read access to claims DB     owner: IT (J. Park)    by Wk1 Fri
    D-2 Service account for policy API owner: IAM team      by Wk2 Wed
    D-3 Two hours a week with handlers owner: Tom (lead)    from Wk3
 6. RACI and how we communicate (demo, status, channel)     10 min
 7. Actions read back, notes sent same day                    5 min

replace_subtopics.title: Weeks 7-10: harden for production
replace_subtopics.body:
Hardening turns a prototype into something people can depend on. It covers error handling (what happens when a call fails), logging (recording what happened for later debugging), data-quality checks, latency and caching, security review, and SLAs (service level agreements, the promised uptime and response times).

A common pattern is to wrap every call to an external system with retries and a timeout, log each attempt in a structured format, and check incoming data before using it. Bad data should be rejected loudly at the edge instead of producing wrong answers quietly.

Also agree who is on call, meaning who gets woken up if something breaks, and write that into a runbook (a step-by-step guide for operating and fixing the system).

Only retry errors that can fix themselves. A timeout, a dropped connection, a 429 (too many requests) or a 5xx server error may succeed a second later. A 400 (bad request), 401 (not logged in) or 404 (not found) will fail the same way every time, so retrying only adds delay and extra load. The retry_if_exception filter in the code does exactly this. Note also that stop_after_attempt(3) means three attempts in total, which is two retries, not three.
replace_subtopics.example: During hardening you find that the policy lookup service times out about once per 500 calls, and that 2% of claims arrive with an empty vehicle registration. You allow up to three attempts (the first try plus two retries) with exponential backoff, only for timeouts and server errors, and route claims with a missing registration to a manual queue. Both show up as counts on the monitoring dashboard.

replace_subtopics.title: Measure against the criteria
replace_subtopics.body:
At the end of hardening, measure the result the same way you measured the baseline: same query, same data source, same definition. Changing the definition midway makes the comparison meaningless and the customer will notice.

Report the number, the comparison to the target, and anything that affected it, such as a holiday week or a system outage. If you missed the target, say so plainly and explain what you learned. A clear miss with a credible plan is better than a fuzzy success.

This measured result is the evidence your account team uses to renew and expand the contract.

Check that both periods have a start and an end date. A filter such as 'everything before 5 January' silently includes years of old claims, which is not the 90-day baseline you agreed in week 1. Both windows in the query below are bounded on both sides.
replace_subtopics.example: Using the week-1 query restricted to the pilot team and weeks 9-10, the median motor triage time is 0.9 hours against a 4.1-hour baseline and a 1-hour target. The p90 dropped from 9.5 to 3.2 hours. You present both numbers to the sponsor along with the list of claims still handled manually.
replace_subtopics.code:
-- Same definition as the baseline, before vs. after
WITH t AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN received_at >= DATE '2026-01-05' - INTERVAL '90 days'
              AND received_at <  DATE '2026-01-05' THEN 'baseline'   -- same 90 days as week 1
         WHEN received_at >= DATE '2026-03-02'
              AND received_at <  DATE '2026-03-16' THEN 'pilot_wk9_10'
    END AS period,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600 AS hours
  FROM claims
  WHERE team = 'motor' AND triaged_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT period,
       COUNT(*) AS claims,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY hours) AS median_hours,
       percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY hours) AS p90_hours
FROM t
WHERE period IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY period;

replace_subtopics.title: Weeks 11-12: handover and a client CoE
replace_subtopics.body:
Handover means the customer can run, fix and extend the system without you. The course calls the receiving team a client Center of Excellence (CoE): a small group of trained owners inside the customer who become the local experts.

A handover package includes documentation, a runbook, access and credentials transferred to customer owners, a training session with a recorded walkthrough, and a support path for the first few weeks.

Finally, write up what you learned for your own product team. Which parts did you have to build that the product should have had? This is the discovery half of the dual-value loop: delivery for the customer, and discovery for your company.

Hypercare is the period of extra support right after go-live. It should end on agreed exit criteria, not on a date alone. Typical criteria: two weeks in a row with no SEV1 (the most severe incident level), the CoE has resolved at least one drill or real incident using the runbook without your help, open defects are below an agreed number, and the usage metric is stable.

After handover, support is usually split into levels. L1 (level 1) is the first contact, often the customer's service desk or CoE: they answer how-to questions and run known fixes from the runbook. L2 is the customer's technical owners: they investigate logs, data problems and configuration. L3 is your company's engineering or product team, for real bugs in the product. Write down who is L1, L2 and L3 and how a ticket moves between them. The supportops topic covers support tiers and SLAs in depth, and the enablement topic covers training the CoE.
replace_subtopics.example: In week 11 you train two engineers and one claims lead at the insurer. They run the weekly retraining themselves while you watch, then fix a staged failure using the runbook. In week 12 you hand over on-call and send your product team a note: three other customers will need the same policy-lookup connector. Hypercare at the insurer was planned to end on 20 April. On 14 April the criteria are met: no SEV1 since 30 March, the CoE fixed a staged policy API outage alone, and only two low defects are open. The sponsor signs the hypercare exit note and L3 tickets now go through the vendor support portal.

    - {name: "L. Chen", role: "data engineer", trained: 2026-03-17}
    - {name: "T. Hale", role: "claims lead (business owner)", trained: 2026-03-18}
  documents:

    - retraining_guide.md
  access_transferred: [cloud_project, monitoring, model_registry]
  drills:

  on_call_owner_from: 2026-03-23
  hypercare_until: 2026-04-20   # vendor support window after go-live

  - "Policy lookup connector: 3 more customers use the same system"
  - "Manual-queue routing rules should be configurable, not coded"

[x] CoE solved a drill alone        policy API outage, 18 min
[x] Open defects <= 3, none high    2 low
[x] Usage stable for 2 weeks        acceptance 71%, 73%

add_subtopics.title: Go-live: readiness and cutover
add_subtopics.body:
Between hardening (weeks 7-10) and measuring there is a launch step: moving from a pilot that some people try to a system people depend on. Skipping it is how good pilots fail on the first day.

The usual path is: UAT (user acceptance testing), where the pilot users run agreed test scripts and sign off that it works for them; a go/no-go meeting, where the sponsor, customer IT and your pod check a readiness list and decide; then a staged rollout. Staged means you widen use step by step. First shadow mode, where the AI makes suggestions in the background and nobody acts on them, so you can compare them with what people actually did. Then one team uses it for real. Then all teams.

Every step needs a rollback plan: how to switch back to the old way of working in minutes, and who is allowed to decide that. On launch day, a run sheet lists each task with a time and an owner, so nobody wonders what happens next.

This is a short summary. The golive topic (Implementation: UAT, cutover and go-live) covers environments, data migration, UAT scripts, the customer's change board, cutover plans and the first week live in full detail.
add_subtopics.example: At the insurer, handlers sign UAT on 24 test claims in week 10. Shadow mode runs for three days and agrees with the handlers on 88% of claims. The go/no-go meeting says go for team A only. On day 2 the policy API slows down, the on-call engineer follows the rollback plan and switches team A back to manual triage for 40 minutes, then re-enables it.

GO / NO-GO CHECKLIST (week 10)

[x] Shadow mode: agreement with handlers >= 85%   (88%)
[x] Rollback tested: switch to manual triage in < 15 min
[x] Runbook and on-call rota named
[ ] Home team trained        -> not needed: team A only
Decision: GO for team A; all teams after 2 clean weeks

LAUNCH-DAY RUN SHEET

08:15 Check dashboard and error rate      owner: Jo
09:00 Check-in with team lead Tom         owner: Maya
12:00 Go/rollback review                  owner: sponsor + Maya

The first meeting of an engagement, where goals, success criteria, plan, roles and dependencies are agreed.
UAT

replace_subtopics.title: Pod anatomy: one Echo, two Deltas
replace_subtopics.body:
The Echo is the Deployment Strategist. They own the customer relationship, run scoping, manage stakeholders, write status reports, chase access requests and handle contracts and scheduling. They are technical enough to understand trade-offs but spend most of their time with people.

The Deltas are the engineers. They build, integrate, debug and deploy. Two engineers give the pod enough capacity to build and cover for each other, while staying small enough that coordination is cheap.

A clear split of responsibilities avoids confusion. A RACI chart is a simple tool for this: for each activity it names who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome), Consulted and Informed.

Echo and Delta are Palantir's internal names, which this course borrows. Other companies shape FDE work differently. A common shape is a customer team where the FDE is paired with an account executive (who owns the commercial relationship and the contract) and a solutions engineer (who runs technical sales and demos before the deal is signed), so the account executive and FDE share the Echo's work. Some companies have a solo FDE who covers several smaller accounts at once and relies on the customer's own engineers. Larger teams have an FDE manager who looks after many pods or accounts, handles staffing and escalations, and coaches the engineers. The role names change, but the questions a RACI chart answers do not: who owns the customer, who builds, and who decides on scope.
replace_subtopics.example: A pod starts at a national grocery chain. The Echo, Maya, runs the weekly steering meeting with the supply chain director and handles the security questionnaire. The Deltas, Ravi and Jo, build the demand forecast pipeline. When the director asks for a new report, Maya takes the request, checks it against the success metric and decides with the sponsor before it reaches the engineers. At a software company selling to mid-sized retailers, one FDE, Sam, supports four accounts. For each account an account executive handles renewals and pricing, so Sam spends his week building and fixing integrations. His FDE manager oversees eight FDEs and steps in when two accounts need Sam in the same week.

# RACI for one pod (R = does it, A = owns outcome, C = consulted, I = informed)
activity:                 echo   delta_1  delta_2  customer_sponsor
  scoping_and_metrics:     A,R     C        C        C
  stakeholder_updates:     A,R     I        I        I
  access_and_security:     A,R     C        C        C
  data_pipeline:           I       A,R      R        I
  model_and_app:           I       R        A,R      I
  weekly_user_demo:        A       R        R        C
  scope_changes:           R       C        C        A

OTHER COMMON SHAPES
shape                         who owns customer       who builds
AE + SE + FDE (per account)   account executive (AE)  FDE (SE before signing)
Solo FDE, 3-5 small accounts  AE for each account     FDE + customer engineers
FDE manager over many pods    each pod lead           pods; manager staffs and escalates

replace_subtopics.title: Darwinistic adoption: ship small, keep what lives
replace_subtopics.body:
Darwinistic adoption is the course's name for letting users decide which features survive. The pod ships small features quickly to real users, measures who uses them, keeps the ones that get adopted and removes the rest.

This replaces a big up-front roadmap inside the account. Instead of predicting what users want, you observe it. It requires instrumentation, meaning the product logs events like 'feature opened' or 'suggestion accepted' so you can count usage.

Set a rule before shipping, such as 'kill it if fewer than 20% of eligible users try it twice within three weeks'. Deciding the threshold in advance stops the team from keeping pet features alive.

Low usage does not always mean low value. Users may not know the feature exists (poor discoverability, for example a button hidden in a menu), or nobody showed them how to use it (missing training). Before removing a feature, talk to three to five eligible users who did not use it. If they say 'I never saw it' or 'I did not know what it was for', fix the placement or the training and measure again. Remove it only if people who know about it still choose not to use it.

Be careful with the time window in the query. A rolling 21-day window (now minus 21 days) can touch four calendar weeks when you group by date_trunc('week', ...), because it starts part-way through one week and ends part-way through the current one. Then '2 of 3 weeks' is really '2 of up to 4'. Use full, completed weeks instead: from the start of the current week minus 21 days, up to (not including) the start of the current week. The query below does this.
replace_subtopics.example: At the grocery chain the pod ships three features in two weeks: a forecast chart, a suggested order quantity and an email alert for likely stockouts. After three weeks, 78% of store managers use suggested orders weekly, 41% open the chart and 6% open the email. The email is removed and suggested orders get the next round of work. Before removing the email alert, Jo calls four store managers who never opened it. Three say it went to a shared inbox nobody reads, so the pod tries sending it to personal inboxes for two weeks. Usage stays under 10%, so the alert is removed with a clear reason.
replace_subtopics.code:
-- Weekly adoption per feature over the last 3 full weeks
WITH eligible AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM users WHERE role = 'store_manager'
),
weeks AS (                      -- the last 3 full, completed weeks
  SELECT date_trunc('week', now()) - INTERVAL '21 days' AS start_ts,
         date_trunc('week', now())                      AS end_ts
),
active AS (
  SELECT feature, user_id
  FROM (
    SELECT feature, user_id, date_trunc('week', ts) AS wk
    FROM events, weeks
    WHERE ts >= weeks.start_ts AND ts < weeks.end_ts
    GROUP BY feature, user_id, date_trunc('week', ts)
  ) w
  GROUP BY feature, user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2          -- used in at least 2 of the 3 full weeks
)
SELECT feature,
       COUNT(*)::float / (SELECT n FROM eligible) AS adoption,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(*)::float / (SELECT n FROM eligible) < 0.2
            THEN 'remove' ELSE 'keep' END AS decision
FROM active
GROUP BY feature
ORDER BY adoption DESC;

add_subtopics.title: Pod rituals and the home team
add_subtopics.body:
A pod works at the customer, but it still belongs to a home team: the product, platform engineering and other pods at your own company. Good rituals keep both sides connected.

A daily pod sync is 15 minutes: what each person did, what they will do, and what is blocked. Blockers that need the customer go to the Echo; blockers inside your own product go to the home team. A weekly sync with product and platform engineering shares what customers are asking for and what broke.

When you find a bug in your company's platform, escalate it properly. Write a ticket with steps to reproduce, the impact on the customer, the version, and a workaround if you have one. Tag the owning team and agree a severity. A clear ticket gets fixed; a message that only says 'it is broken' gets lost.

Code review happens inside the pod too. One Delta reviews the other's changes before they reach the customer, even under time pressure. Pods also share a knowledge base of connectors, prompts, runbooks and lessons learned, so the next pod does not solve the same problem again.

People rotate between accounts. Handing an account over means a written handover note (the customer's people, open risks, promises made, where the code and docs are) and at least one joint customer meeting where the new person is introduced. The asyncwriting topic covers writing handover notes and end-of-day updates.
add_subtopics.example: At the grocery chain, Ravi finds that the platform's CSV importer drops rows with accented store names. He writes a ticket with a 5-row sample file, notes that 40 stores are affected and that renaming the file encoding is a workaround, and tags platform engineering as severity 2. It is fixed in the next release, and the workaround is added to the shared knowledge base.
